_: The standard world — what a place is made of on any beach, and the underscore each block is born carrying. A play surface is NAMED BLOCKS AT A URL and nothing else — no engine to install, no world-server to run — so a world comes into being as ordinary bsp() writes from any door, exactly as a shell does; its shape is one of FOUR (the family at 1.5: spine, compact, seed, table), and FIT is a property of PLACEMENT, never of content — an address on a world spine plus the inheritance law, the finer bound by the coarser (the graft at 2.4). Read this before authoring one. Two halves, told apart by who consumes them: the DEFINITION at 2-5, authored once and read-only while anyone plays, and the OPENING SAVE at 6, which play consumes and replaces. The composition companion to shell-genome — that one says what an inhabitant is made of, this one says what the place they inhabit is made of, and the two meet at a character's location star-ref. The law at 1 governs whether a second group can ever play what the first group played, and is the thing most often got wrong.

1._: THE SCENARIO·TABLE LAW — canon is authored, tables are played, and the two are never the same surface. A world authored for others to play is a SCENARIO: read-only, the fixed scaffolding, nobody's story in it yet. A group plays at a TABLE — their own surface at <beach>/w/<scenario>-<group> — where their characters live and their pools accumulate. Nothing done at a table touches canon or any other group's table, so a million groups play the same scenario concurrently and each has its own ending. Replay is a fresh table name and nothing else. The two nouns are all a player needs: the scenario they were pointed at, and the table they play in.
1.1: A scenario played in place stops being replayable, and the damage is silent. Every consequence a beat writes back — a door now open, an object taken, a mark added, a character standing in a room — lands in the definition blocks, where the next group inherits it as scenery they did not earn. The demonstrated case is the-reaper (authored and played on one surface, July 2026): its spatial block carries the closet already emptied, a fourth tally already scratched, and a rescued figure standing in the bathroom doorway, alongside two characters who belong to a finished story. Nothing failed loudly; the surface still reads as a scenario and still opens. A group forking it today would arrive after the ending. A scenario that has been played is a spent table wearing canon's URL, and the only repair is to move the play off it and re-author the opening state.
1.2: REFERENCE, not copy — a table holds only what the group makes. The characters (passport, purpose, history, stash per shell-genome) and the room pools live at the table; the place does not. A character's location is already a star-ref — passport position 3 carries 'Location: *:<canon beach>:spatial:<world>:<addr>' — so pointing that ref at the SCENARIO makes the place shared and read-only by nature, and a Character cannot pollute what it never writes to. No fork, no nine hand-copies, no dropped block, no drift between a table's copy and a canon that has since been re-authored. The isolation that matters is preserved exactly, because the isolation that matters is play-state, and play-state is per-table.
1.3: A frozen copy stays available, and is a deliberate act rather than the default. Where a playtest must not move under its players — a scenario being re-authored while a group is mid-campaign, or a run whose conditions have to be reproducible — the table takes a verbatim whole-block copy of every definition block instead of referencing them. Copy CONTENT, never locks: the structure read is the structure written, unchanged, and the copy is checked block-name against block-name before anyone arrives, because a dropped block does not fail at copy time, it fails as a Character stopping mid-genesis with a piece of the world missing. Choosing copy is choosing to inherit the scenario's bugs for the run's duration; that is sometimes exactly what is wanted.
1.4: AUTHOR prepares, CHARACTER plays, and one seat never does both in one breath. Preparing a table shapes what others inhabit and needs rigor; genesis and play are free, immersed, and low-stakes. Fusing them is what pollutes canon — a seat reading the scenario from one beach while writing a character to another fills the write-target with the beach it was READING, and the character lands on canon. The lead player wears Author once, finishing before anyone sits down, then joins as a Character like everyone else. Where a table is already prepared, no player ever reads canon at all, and the failure cannot occur. The ownership seam runs the same way through every surface shape: AUTHOR owns place and folk — the registers at 2, the roster, the keeper; DESIGNER owns the rules mounts, the frame-spec and the locks; CHARACTER owns nothing on a world surface — a character's own blocks are shell-genome's business and live at the table.

5._: THE FOUR SURFACE SHAPES the law composes into — every play surface is one of these, told apart by which halves it carries and by whether play may write to it. Choosing the shape is the first authoring decision, before any block is written, because the shape decides the roster: which of the blocks at 2-6 stand at the surface and which are reached through a placing instead. The concrete writes for minting each shape stand at a beach's ways:authoring branch 8 where one is hosted; the anatomy each roster names is this block's own branches.
5.1: THE WORLD SPINE — the registers only, at a surface of their own: spatial, temporal, identity and keeper of the world (2 and 5), no rooms, no characters, no door blocks. Play never lands here; bubbles and tables carry all play and bind back through the placing star-ref (keeper position 3), inheriting the spine coarse-to-fine at every engage. Pure canon at the coarsest grain, so the Author face owns the whole surface, and standing is an operator act — a line in the beach's worlds register, a sub-domain where granted. The worked model is urb: four blocks, with the gal bubbles playing beneath it.
5.2: THE COMPACT WORLD — registers, rooms and characters on ONE surface, for a world that is one coherent lived-in place rather than a scenario for strangers: the registers at 2 and 5 as the world needs them, rooms mounted on the world's own directive, the residents' blocks beside them. The deliberate exception to playing-where-authored: legitimate exactly where replay-by-strangers is not the point, because a home world accumulates its own consequences as life, not as pollution. Growth runs under the engine through the author lane (grit 8.5), never as a seat's mid-beat invention; a compact world that starts growing bubbles graduates to the spine shape, its registers moving out whole. Worked models: earth, and the-reaper as intended — the recorded failure at 1.1 is not this shape but this shape wearing a scenario's expectations.
5.3: THE SCENARIO SEED — the full kit and no characters: the definition at 2-5 whole, the opening save at 6 empty, and the canon declaration at lighthouse 9.3 — the sign that makes every doorway route an arrival to found a table rather than play in place. Nobody's story is in it yet, and nothing keeps it that way except the sign and the doors that honour it. A variant seed carries provenance at each changed block's position 9: forked-from, what changed, when. The worked model is brackenfoot.
5.4: THE TABLE — what a group actually plays: their characters, their pools, the keeper carrying the placing star-ref at position 3 (per 5), the kit standing as verbatim copies under the founder's lock — the rules blocks, char-creation, the roster, the run's lockfiles — and the gate. Under the REFERENCE model, the default, that is the whole roster: NO spatial, NO identity, no copy of the place at all — the place is read live from the shared master the placing names, room by room at the room's own address, so a Character cannot pollute canon (the place is never on a surface a player writes to) and a re-authored master reaches every table at its next engage. The COPY form remains as the opt-in FREEZE (1.3), a deliberate act under its own name: a table that must not move while the master is re-authored copies the definition whole and reads only itself. gal-fen half-lives the reference shape today — placing live and inherited every engage, local scene content still standing beside it.

2._: THE PUBLIC REGISTERS — the three coordinates anyone at the world may read, and between them the whole of what is objectively there. Everything with a WHY in it belongs at 5 instead. Each is a separate block so a face can be handed one without the others, and so a region can be grafted into a larger world by address without carrying its neighbours — the graft law at 4. All three are AUTHOR territory: coherence is the bar, because others inhabit what stands here.
2.1: spatial:<world> — the places, as a nested skeleton whose floor sets how deep an address runs. A floor of 3 means a three-digit address lands in a room (brackenfoot's Slip at 211: the holding's second region, its first sub-place, its first room), and the digit-path IS the containment, so a walk to 2 gives the region and a walk to 211 gives the room inside it. Standing figures and fixed scenery are prose in the room's own underscore, never separate positions — a figure at its own digit reads as a live co-present character and doubles the scenery. Room pools derive from this: the room a handle meets in is pool:<its address>, so co-located handles share a pool with nothing configured, and a crowded place subdivides by growing a deeper address. Underscore at birth: 'The places of <world>, floor <N> — <the digit-depth legend, coarsest to finest>; <the situation these places imply, in one line>.' — the floor fixed before the first address is written.
2.2: temporal:<world> — the clock, and the grain at which the world's beats fall due. A world may fold this into its rules block instead where the clock is simple; a world with seasons, a reinforcement countdown, or several rates running at once wants it standing separately, because a rate is a thing players negotiate with rather than a rule they obey. The address carries its grain: where the road drops a character is also how fast they live, and a world re-declares the ladder in its rules only when it differs from the standard spine. Underscore at birth, where it stands alone: 'The clock of <world> — <the rates that run at once, and the grain each falls due at>.'
2.3: identity:<world> — how each 'we' holds each place, mirroring the spatial skeleton position for position. Where spatial says what is at an address, identity fans that same address into the several groups who hold it and what each believes about it — villagers, occupying crew, newcomers, and whoever is named only at the count. This is the register that makes a place contested rather than described, and it is what an arriving character's first perception is scoped through. Underscore at birth: 'How each we holds each place of <world> — mirroring spatial:<world> position for position; the groups fan at the places they contest.'
2.4: THE GRAFT — how a region joins a world, and the whole of what FIT means. Fit is a property of PLACEMENT, never of content: a region fits a world when it stands at a proximate address on the world's spatial spine — one step from a named neighbour — and the inheritance law does the rest, the finer bound by the coarser at every rung above it. Small content writes INTO the spatial position itself; substantial content hives off as its own block, star-ref'd from the parent position (block-conventions:4.74), each block supernesting at its own pace. Scenario placings and character locations resolve THROUGH the spine — the placing star-ref names the world's address, and everything beneath inherits everything above — so grafting a region in enlarges every table already bound to the spine, and touches none of them. Expanding a world IS authoring more regions at proximate addresses, an Author act; the fork-and-reset rig a cartridge carries is its private concern, and the blocks graft independently of it.

3._: THE LAW — what decides an uncertain act, kept in two blocks because they are forked by different people for different reasons. A world with no law is not a game: every attempted act simply succeeds, the only cost is whatever the narrating seat chooses to invent, and nothing a player does can fail in a way they did not consent to. That is a story being told at a player rather than a game being played.
3.1: rules:<world> — the place's own physics and its tactical spine, authored with the scenario and forked by whoever runs it. What is true here that is not true everywhere: the standing situation, the clocks that run against the party, the conditions that shift a difficulty (an occupying crew weaker after dark; a rider sent for reinforcement costing three days), and the threads deliberately left unexplained. This is AUTHOR territory — it shapes content, so it must be coherent, because others inhabit it. Underscore at birth: 'What is true in <world> that is not true everywhere — <the standing situation>; <the clocks that run against the party>; <what shifts a difficulty>.'
3.2: rules:nomad — the resolution system, mounted rather than embedded, and the Designer's dial. Capability plus situation plus dice against difficulty, read into bands. It sits as its own block precisely so a table can fork it: a group who wants a grittier game edits their table's copy and no other group is touched, and a group who wants a different system entirely mounts a different block under the same name. This is DESIGNER territory — it must be correct rather than merely coherent, and it is the one place in a world where the rigor of code applies. Mounted means COPIED VERBATIM as a lockfile under the run's own lock, never re-authored in place and never referenced live — the one deliberate copy in the reference model, because a resolution system that moves under a mid-campaign table changes what a staged act means.

4._: THE DOOR — the four blocks that decide what happens to a person who arrives, in the order the arrival meets them. Authoring a world and forgetting these produces a place that reads beautifully and cannot be entered: a visitor gets an index of blocks, no way to become anyone, and no sign saying whether they may play here.
4.1: frame-spec:<world> — the CADO manifest: which blocks each face may read, and how wide an aperture each is handed. Tier picks the frame, face picks the register — so a Character frame naming the held register at 5 is a leak by construction, not a judgement call, and the demonstrated failure is a character arriving already holding names nobody told them. Position 9 carries the window duration, which is how long the room gathers staged intentions before a beat folds. Underscore at birth: 'The CADO manifest of <world> — which blocks each face reads, and how wide an aperture each is handed.' This is DESIGNER territory, with the locks.
4.2: roster:<world> — ready roles a newcomer may adopt, held UNPLACED: no location, no lock, no passport of their own. A role becomes a person only when a player takes it up at genesis and its capability, drive, look and knowings are copied into their own locked blocks. Four roles spanning the scenario's ways through is the working shape — the party's spread and the world's answer to it. A roster is what lets someone say yes to a friend's invitation in one sentence instead of authoring a character from nothing. Underscore at birth: 'Ready roles of <world>, held unplaced — a role becomes a person only at genesis, copied into a player's own locked blocks.'
4.3: char-creation — the genesis interview, hosted here only as a thin delta over the substrate passage at pscale:char-creation. Change only what is world-specific: offer the roster, calibrate in this world's own bands, name the arrival place. Defer the write-and-lock ceremony to the substrate copy rather than restating it, because a restated ceremony drifts and the drift surfaces as a character born without locks. A world that needs no delta hosts nothing and the substrate passage is used whole. Underscore at birth, where a delta is hosted: 'GENESIS at <world> — the substrate passage with this world's own roster and arrival; the ceremony stands at pscale:char-creation.'
4.4: lighthouse — the sign at the front, and the one block that is never copied to a table. Position 9.3 carries the play-disposition, and a value beginning 'canon' declares this surface read-only: the doorway reads it and routes an arriving player to their table instead of opening a gate here. The branches above carry the paths themselves — one for the Character who already has a table and belongs there, one for the Author preparing a table for a group, one for what the door then does for everyone. A table carrying canon's sign would send its own players away, which is why the copy stops here. Underscore at birth: '<WORLD> — <what this surface is in one line, and where play actually happens>.'
4.5: THE DOOR CONTRACT — what a doorway owes an arrival at an EMPTY name, and the rule beneath it: A PLACE IS AUTHORED BEFORE PERSONS. A surface whose index lists no blocks — or none of the place-bearing names: spatial, identity, keeper, pool — receives the AUTHOR PASSAGE, never the character gate: the plain statement that nothing stands at the name; the live lines of the beach's worlds register, so a mistyped name corrects itself before anyone authors a duplicate; this genome, whole; the mint recipe (ways:authoring branch 8, where the beach hosts one); and the first writes of the chosen shape — a bubble placed on an existing spine, or a standalone world begun at its situation. Then the door stops — no gate, no genesis, nothing to inhabit yet. The predicate is EMPTINESS, never incompleteness: a reference table legitimately holds no definition blocks and enters normally by its passports and pools; a surface holding any place-bearing block is a world mid-life, not a blank. The canon sign at lighthouse 9.3 is read before emptiness is ever judged.

5: keeper:<world> — the HELD register, where everything with a why in it lives: what the place is for, what is really going on beneath what anyone can see, which threads are load-bearing and which are decoration, and what the world does when players go somewhere unprepared. The public registers at 2 deliver what is there; this delivers what it means, and the split is the whole of information-hiding in a world — a Character never reads here, an Author does, and the keeper's own frame IS this block. Authoring the scenario without it works, and costs the world its second session: the seat running it re-invents the reason for everything each time, and the reasons do not agree with each other. Position 3 carries the PLACING — the star-ref binding this surface into the world above it, '*:<world-beach-url>:spatial:<world>:<address>' — which every room envelope walks to inherit the world coarse-to-fine, and through which a reference table holding no spatial of its own resolves its whole place (1.54). Underscore at birth: 'The Author's hold for <world> — what is truly afoot, kept from every stranger's envelope; the surface is spatial:<world>, the folk are identity:<world>, and the truth is here.'

6._: THE OPENING SAVE — the two blocks that open EMPTY and are the only ones play writes to. Everything above is authored and then left alone; these are the world's live state, and the entire difference between a scenario and a spent table is whether these have anything in them. Both are unlocked: play is the act of writing here, and a lock at the room's door means nobody can take a turn.
6.1: pool:<arrival address> — the arrival room's event stream, named for the place it is at, opening empty and mounting the play loop at its underscore. A bare reference at that underscore is resolved and delivered inline on every engage, so pointing it at pscale:grit hands every seat the perceive-act-commit discipline without a per-world copy to drift. A world needs exactly one pool authored — the arrival room — because every other room's pool is created by the first character who walks there. Underscore at birth: the mount alone — 'pscale:grit/1' — and nothing else; the reference IS the purpose, and prose beside it would stop the resolver reading it as a mount.
6.2: liquid:pool:<arrival address> — the staging window beside it, opening empty. One slot per author, overwriting, cleared as each beat folds: what is staged here is intention, revisable and private to the moment, and what lands in the pool beside it is the committed act. This is also how a room answers who is here right now, which is the question a scenario cannot answer for a group and the group cannot answer without it. No underscore to author at birth: the buffer writes its own on the first stage, and the window-open stamp lives there.

7._: AUTHORING ONE, from any door — the walk, in the order that makes each step decidable from the last. The SHAPE is chosen before the walk begins (the four at 1.5), and the shape decides which steps apply whole: a seed or a compact world walks all of them; a spine stops at the registers; a table founds by placing and kit instead, per 1.54. Then: the place before the law, because what can go wrong here is what the rules must resolve; the law before the door, because the roster is calibrated in the rules' own bands; and the sign last, because it declares finished work read-only. Each step is ordinary bsp() writes, locked under one passphrase the author chooses and never echoes back. Where the beach hosts ways:authoring, its branch 8 is the mint recipe — each shape's writes in full, ready to copy. Ten blocks and the world is complete and enterable; a world can be authored well in an hour and badly in five minutes, and the difference shows up in the second session, never the first.
7.1: Start from the situation, not the map. A scenario is a place with something already wrong in it that the arriving party is positioned to meet — write that first as a paragraph of prose, then let the spatial skeleton be the places that paragraph implies. Authoring geography first produces a well-formed world with nothing at stake in it, which reads as thorough and plays as empty. Fix the floor before writing any address (how deep a room sits), because a floor change afterwards moves every address in identity, in the roster's placements, and in every pool name derived from them.
7.2: Write the arrival last among the places and hardest. Every character enters here, so it carries the whole first impression, must be enterable by strangers who agreed nothing beforehand, and must offer at least two directions that are visibly not the same. Name it in the lighthouse and in char-creation identically; a mismatch surfaces as a character born at an address that names no place, and the doorway refuses entry with nowhere to go.
7.3: Check the ten before anyone arrives, by listing the surface and reading the names back. The definition blocks are spatial, temporal where the clock stands alone, identity, rules:<world>, rules:nomad, frame-spec, roster, char-creation, keeper, lighthouse; the opening save is the arrival pool and its liquid. A missing block does not fail at authoring time — it fails at the worst possible moment, when a player is mid-genesis and a piece of the world is absent. Then validate the shapes against pscale:well-formed, whose mechanical half the beach already enforces and whose interpretive half no gate will catch for you.
7.4: Then stop being the Author. Registering the world in the beach's worlds directory is one authored line and makes the name resolvable; it is not required, and a scenario shared by URL alone is complete. From here the preparer is a player like the others and walks the door exactly as they do — and the first thing that door should do is send them to a table, because the surface just authored is canon now, and the law at 1 applies to its author first. Growth after the sign is the author LANE, not a return to the workbench: orders thrown from play land at the world's order block, and an Author collects and generates under the engine — rolled from the world's own ladders, grounded by its fence, register-split public and held (grit 8.5) — so the world grows in play without any seat inventing canon mid-beat.
